Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

Growth has decisively beaten value and defensives over the past month. US Info Tech is +6.64% over 1m and +27.02% YTD, and Comm Services is +4.7% over 1m and led the prior session at +1.92%. Global Info Tech is +34.46% YTD. Rate-sensitive defensives are being crushed by 5%+ long yields. US Utilities are -8.71% over 1m and -8.86% YTD, Real Estate -7.36% over 1m, and Cons Staples -3.9% over 1m. Cyclicals are weak too: Materials -6.99% (US) and -7.75% (global) over 1m, Industrials -5.2%, Cons Discr -5.28%, and Financials -6.25% over 1m in the US and -2.05% over 1w. Financials' weakness alongside tight credit spreads is a divergence worth watching. Energy is the only non-tech group with positive 1m returns (US +1.32%, global +1.17%) and leads YTD (US +36.76%, global +33.22%), reflecting the Iran oil shock, though it lagged over 1w (-2.31% US). The pattern is a narrow, AI-led market in which higher rates punish bond-proxies and cyclicals alike. That is late-cycle leadership concentration, not a broad risk-on rotation.

🧮Fixed Income Spreadscomputed

Credit is priced for perfection. US IG OAS is 0.77% (z -0.83, 3rd percentile, historic range 0.71–6.18) and US HY OAS 2.82% (z -0.84, 10th percentile, range 2.33–19.71). EUR IG is 0.87% (16th percentile), EUR HY 2.95% (13th percentile), and EM USD OAS 1.56% (z -1.41, 2nd percentile). All computed. The vs_crisis readings are 0 across GFC 2008, EuroDebt 2011, COVID 2020 and Hike 2022, so current spreads are nowhere near any past stress episode. Spreads did tick wider in the latest print (US IG +0.01, US HY +0.08, EUR HY +0.09, EM +0.04). Key levels: the IG floor is the 0.71% historic minimum, which would need a further disinflationary soft landing plus continued equity melt-up. Around 1.0% IG and 3.5% HY would signal repricing, likely triggered by a Warsh hike that tightens financial conditions or a sustained Brent spike. Crisis-type widening toward mid-single-digit HY would require recession plus a funding shock, which is not in the data today. With a 5%+ 10Y, all-in corporate yields are high even though spreads are thin, and that is what is keeping buyers in.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +1.16 vol points (96th percentile of the 27 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 104.6 (76th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 101bp (steeper by 40bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE
Left rim6.79%2000-01-20
Cup base0.51%2020-08-04
Right rim5.20%2026-09-24

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 75% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (99bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.20 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 75%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Moderately persistent, and core is gradually cooling. The core-trend measures sit mid-distribution and most are falling (computed), so underlying inflation is not re-accelerating. The problem is the level and the energy shock. Core PCE is 3.34% YoY versus Core CPI at 2.4%, and flexible CPI is running 4.94% because of the oil shock. Breadth is mixed: 22.3% of the PCE basket is rising faster than 5% (>10%: 9.3, 5–10%: 13.0), while 25.8% is falling. That justifies Warsh's hawkish lean without signalling a wage-price spiral.

Today looks less like March 2000 and more like 1998–99: a narrow AI/semis mania inside a complacent but not yet euphoric market, with a hawkish Fed as the catalyst to watch.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Using the computed indicators, the bubble signal is concentrated rather than broad. Valuation extremes sit in the leadership group (semis), market concentration is high (top-10 about 38% of the S&P 500), and aggregate measures are rich: Shiller CAPE about 41 and market cap/GDP about 238–244% per public trackers. Those are analyst-sourced figures, not computed. What has not happened yet is the 2000 endgame: an inverted curve, rolling PMIs, euphoric retail sentiment and an IPO frenzy. The US IPO calendar this week could not be verified, and IPO froth is judged moderate (analyst estimate). The drawdown template is sobering: the Nasdaq fell 78.0% from 5048.62 (2000-03-10) to 1114.11 (2002-10-09) over 31 months. On the chart overlay, the current cycle (anchored Oct-2022) is at month 47 with the index at 245.2. The 1994-anchored dot-com path peaked at month 69 near 665, and the valuation marker sits at 22% of the peak P/E. If the analog holds, there is time, not safety. Warsh's willingness to hike into loose financial conditions is the most plausible catalyst to turn complacency into repricing.

⚔️Iran War

The US-Israel war with Iran is in its seventh month with no breakthrough. At the UN General Assembly, President Pezeshkian became the first leader of a country at war with the US to address the body. He left the door open to negotiations while condemning the US blockade in the Strait of Hormuz (CBS News). Trump said US envoys met Iranian officials for about three hours on the sidelines, but analysts judge a deal this week unlikely because core disagreements remain (CBS News). Rhetoric escalated. In response to Trump's annihilation threat, a senior adviser to the supreme leader warned that Iran and the Houthis could open 'a new front' targeting Red Sea energy supplies (CBS News). A commercial vessel was struck in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, killing one crew member and forcing the evacuation of more than 20 others (CBS News). Tehran said it hopes the US returns to a memorandum of understanding and 'won't be bullied' but remains open to talks (Al Jazeera, Sept 24). Market read: Brent at 104.98 still embeds a large war premium. This morning's -1.62 decline looks like positioning relief, not de-escalation, and the Red Sea 'new front' threat is the key upside oil risk.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Next meeting: a hawkish hold with a live hike bias, and a 25bp hike is a genuine possibility (analyst inference). Warsh's Jackson Hole speech gave a more hawkish reading of inflation, recommitted to the 2% PCE target and was read as raising hike odds. At the Sept 16 press conference he said financial conditions were 'not restrictive'. With NFCI at -0.56 (loose), IG spreads at the 3rd percentile and equities at 100th-percentile trend extremes (all computed), his own framework points toward tightening.

~1 YEAR

About one year out: policy rates are likely held at or modestly above current levels (analyst inference), with the path set by financial conditions rather than forward guidance, which he has abandoned. Balance-sheet shrinkage is a stated goal but is moving slowly as he seeks consensus. Expect gradual runoff rather than an abrupt QT step-up. Rate cuts are unlikely unless core PCE (3.34%) converges toward the ~2.3–2.7% trimmed/median measures.

Warsh has run a regime change at the Fed. He dropped traditional forward guidance, elevated broad financial conditions as a policy input and refocused on the 2% PCE target (CNBC, NPR). He has said short-term rates remain the main tool and that AI and balance-sheet questions are not driving near-term policy (CNBC, Jackson Hole). His reforms are meeting internal resistance (CNBC, Sept 25), and analysts note a hawkish Fed may be 'at odds' with Treasury (CNBC, Aug 31). Inference: because he targets financial conditions, rallies in equities and credit make a hike more likely, not less. That is a key asymmetry for risk assets at current extremes.

Sources: Warsh's regime change at the Fed pushes ahead – and meets resistance — CNBC (2026-09-25) · Kevin Warsh sharpens inflation warning at Jackson Hole, signaling possible rate hike — CNBC · Jackson Hole analyst roundup: Warsh's speech sends hike chances higher — CNBC · Fed Chair Kevin Warsh warns inflation is still too high — NPR · Warsh Sounds Hawkish, but Will There Be a September Rate Hike? — Morningstar
